vocabulary.term: Rational Numbers on the Number Line
vocabulary.termEs: Números racionales en la recta numérica
vocabulary.definition: Every rational number has one exact spot on the number line. Writing it as a fraction, a decimal, or an integer does not change where it sits.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cada número racional tiene un lugar exacto en la recta numérica. Escribirlo como fracción, decimal o entero no cambia dónde queda.
vocabulary.visual: −3/2 = −1.5 and 1/2 = 0.5 each sit at one exact point.
vocabulary.cloze: A rational number always has one exact spot on the ___ ___.

examples.why: Its value decides where it goes, not its form.
The digits are not the value — -3/4 is less than one unit from 0.

vocabulary.definition: A number that can be written as a fraction of two integers, with a bottom number that is not zero.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número que se puede escribir como una fracción de dos enteros, con un denominador que no sea cero.
vocabulary.visual: −1/2, 0 and 5/4 each sit at one exact point.
vocabulary.cloze: A number you can write as a fraction of two integers, with a bottom number that is not zero, is a ___.

examples.why: It can be written as −3/1 — both parts are integers.
It can be written as 3/4, so it is rational.

vocabulary.definition: A number that shows part of a whole, like 3/4.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número que muestra una parte de un todo, como 3/4.
vocabulary.visual: 3/4 means 3 out of 4 equal parts — like 3 slices of a pizza cut into 4
vocabulary.cloze: A number that shows part of a whole, like 3/5, is a ___.

examples.text: -3/4 as a point three-quarters of the way from 0 to -1
examples.why: It names a part of a whole and has a place on the line.
Two separate digits are not a part of a whole.

vocabulary.definition: A number with a dot, like 0.5, that shows a part less than one.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número con un punto, como 0.5, que muestra una parte menor que uno.
vocabulary.visual: 0.5 = 1/2 (halfway between 0 and 1 on the number line)
vocabulary.cloze: A number that uses a point to show parts of a whole is a ___.

examples.why: The decimal part places it between two integers.
Dropping the point changes the value entirely.

vocabulary.definition: A straight line where numbers are placed in order; numbers get smaller to the left and larger to the right.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una recta donde los números se colocan en orden; los números son menores a la izquierda y mayores a la derecha.
vocabulary.cloze: A line with numbers in order used to place and compare values is a ___.

examples.text: A line with -3, 0 and 3 marked in order
examples.why: Values placed in order, left to right, around 0.

examples.text: Three numbers listed in a column

vocabulary.definition: Having the same value, just written a different way.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Tener el mismo valor, escrito de otra forma.
vocabulary.visual: 1/2 = 0.5 = 2/4 — all name the same point on the number line

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Andrew's Reasoning about Opposites
revealWordProblem.text:
Andrew made the generalization about opposite numbers shown on the note: if x and y are both greater than 0 and x < y, then −x > −y.
Question: Do you agree with Andrew's statement? Explain your reasoning using a number line.
revealWordProblem.imageAlt: A sticky note reading: If x and y are both greater than 0 and x is less than y, then negative x is greater than negative y.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: I agree. Try numbers first: let x = 2 and y = 5, so x < y is true. Their opposites are −2 and −5, and on a number line −2 sits to the right of −5, so −2 > −5, which is exactly what Andrew claims. This works every time: taking the opposite reflects each number across 0, so the number that was closer to 0 on the right is still closer to 0 on the left — and on a number line the number farther right is greater. So the smaller positive always has the greater opposite.

That value is positive, which puts it on the right side of 0. Both -1 and -2 sit to the left of 0, so the number you need is negative.

reviewHighlights.watchOut: A common mistake in Rational Numbers on the Number Line is treating the numerator and denominator of a negative fraction as two separate whole numbers instead of one value between two integers — for example, plotting -3/4 by going to -3 and then counting 4 more units to the left, landing (incorrectly) at -7, instead of recognizing that -3/4 = -0.75, which sits between 0 and -1. level2.stem: Which rational number is closest to 0 on the number line?
level2.explanation: |-1/4| = 0.25, |0.5| = 0.5, |-2| = 2, |1.75| = 1.75. Since 0.25 is the smallest absolute value, -1/4 is closest to zero.
choiceFeedback: |0.5| = 0.5, but one negative option sits even closer to zero than that. Distance ignores sign — compare absolute values before ruling out the negatives.
Distance from 0 is what matters here, and this number sits a full 2 units away. Compare absolute values rather than signs.
This value is almost 2 units from 0. Convert every option to a decimal and compare how far each one is from zero, ignoring direction.
hints: 'Closest to 0' means the SMALLEST distance from zero — the sign doesn't matter.
Find each choice's absolute value — for example |0.5| = 0.5 — then look for the smallest distance.
Write every choice as a distance from zero, then compare all four distances and take the smallest.

level2.explanationEs: |-1/4| = 0.25, |0.5| = 0.5, |-2| = 2, |1.75| = 1.75. Como 0.25 es el valor absoluto más pequeño, -1/4 es el más cercano a cero.
hintsEs: 'Más cerca de 0' significa la MENOR distancia desde cero; el signo no importa.

Empieza con dos: |−1/4| = 0.25 y |0.5| = 0.5. Halla las otras dos distancias y compara las cuatro.

Zero is its own opposite and sits at the center. The opposite of a number is the same distance from 0, just on the other side.

level3.stemEs: Ordena estos tres marcadores del sendero de menor a mayor: -1.5, 0.5, -0.5.
level3.explanationEs: El que está más a la izquierda en la recta numérica va primero: -1.5, luego -0.5 y después 0.5.
hints: Least to greatest means left to right on the number line.
Split the markers into negatives and positives first — every negative is less than every positive.
Among the negatives, -1.5 is farther from 0 than -0.5, so it sits farther left. Place those two in order, then add the positive marker.
hintsEs: De menor a mayor significa de izquierda a derecha en la recta numérica.
Separa primero los marcadores en negativos y positivos: todo negativo es menor que todo positivo.
Entre los negativos, -1.5 está más lejos de 0 que -0.5, así que queda más a la izquierda. Coloca esos dos en orden y luego agrega el marcador positivo.
